view.stem: Which statements about ordinary specular reflection at a smooth mirror are correct? Each normal is the local normal at the point of incidence; non-normal incidence means that the incident ray is not along that normal.

options.text: At non-normal incidence, the incident ray, reflected ray and normal are coplanar, with the rays on opposite sides of the normal.
The incidence and reflection angles should be defined as the respective ray angles to the tangent surface at the point of incidence.
At non-normal incidence, the incident and reflected rays are coplanar, with both rays on the same side of the normal.
The incidence and reflection angles are each measured from the local normal at the point of incidence, and are equal.
At non-normal incidence, the plane determined by the incident ray and normal is perpendicular to the plane determined by the reflected ray and normal.
At normal incidence, both incidence and reflection angles are zero, and the reflected ray returns along the original straight line.

intent.task: Collectively judge the complete reflection law's coplanarity, local-normal angle convention, equality of angles and non-normal side relation, including the degenerate normal-incidence case.
intent.source_solution: The full independent solution was frozen before option-bearing draft files were written. For ordinary specular reflection, the incident ray, reflected ray and local normal are coplanar; at non-normal incidence the ray branches are on opposite sides of the normal. Incidence and reflection angles are measured from the normal and are equal. At normal incidence both angles are zero and the reflected ray retraces the incoming straight path; the incidence plane is not unique, but coplanarity can still hold. Reflection preserves the tangential component of the incoming propagation direction and reverses its normal component, yielding a direction in the incident-direction/normal plane and equal geometric ray-branch angles to the normal. Equal complementary angles to the tangent surface describe equivalent geometry but are not the standard named-angle definitions.
intent.unit_reason: The source asks for one full law with coupled constraints. One native multiple unit judges its conditions and normal-incidence limit together instead of separate yes/no fragments. Six statements express the correct conditions and three specific mistaken procedures; neither definition count nor an item quota determines the response count.
limitations: Selecting correct statements does not demonstrate unaided oral or written recitation or a complete independently produced explanation of the law.
The scope is ordinary geometric-optics specular reflection; no material reflectivity, wave amplitude or refraction task is added.
There is no corresponding whitelisted definition paragraph, so the full standalone conceptual seed is used without importing solved constructions as definitions.

rationales.derivation: Reflection preserves the tangential propagation component and reverses the normal component, so both directions lie in the incident-direction/normal plane. As geometric branches pointing away from the point of incidence toward the source and reflected side, the rays are on opposite sides of the normal at non-normal incidence.

The standard incidence and reflection angles are measured between each ray and the local normal. Angles to the tangent surface are their complements; equal complements may describe equivalent reflection geometry, but do not redefine the standard named angles.
rationales.misconception: Use the visible tangent surface as the reference, substitute its complementary ray angles for normal angles, and incorrectly label those complements incidence and reflection angles.

rationales.derivation: At non-normal incidence the incident and reflected ray branches are symmetric about the normal in the incidence plane and lie on opposite sides. Coplanarity does not replace this by a same-side relationship.
rationales.misconception: Keep only coplanarity, copy the geometric branch toward the source onto the same side of the normal as the reflected branch, and omit the symmetry transformation across the normal.

rationales.derivation: The local normal is the standard reference for both named angles. Reflection reverses the normal component without changing its magnitude and preserves the tangential component, making the acute geometric branch angles equal; both are zero at normal incidence.
At non-normal incidence the incident-ray/normal plane is also the reflected-ray/normal plane, not a separate perpendicular plane.
rationales.misconception: Find the incidence plane, preserve the angle to the normal, but rotate the reflected ray by a quarter turn around the normal, incorrectly treating equal angles as permission to change to a perpendicular plane.

rationales.derivation: At normal incidence the incoming direction is along the normal and its tangential component is zero. Reflection reverses the normal propagation direction without introducing a tangential component, so it returns along the same line with both named angles zero.

view.stem: In the paraxial approximation, which statement correctly describes the principal focuses of concave and convex mirrors? In front means on the incident-light side of the mirror.

options.text: After axis-parallel rays reflect, a concave mirror's reflected rays extend backward to a virtual principal focus behind the mirror; a convex mirror's reflected rays actually meet at a real principal focus in front.
After axis-parallel rays reflect, a concave mirror's reflected rays meet at a real principal focus in front; a convex mirror's actual reflected rays meet at a real principal focus behind the mirror.

After axis-parallel rays reflect, a concave mirror's reflected rays meet at a real principal focus in front; a convex mirror's reflected rays extend backward to a virtual principal focus behind the mirror.

After axis-parallel rays reflect, a concave mirror's reflected rays meet at the curvature center in front as a real principal focus; a convex mirror's reflected rays extend backward to the curvature center behind as a virtual principal focus.

intent.task: Recognize a complete spherical-mirror principal-focus definition, preserving axis-parallel incidence, the paraxial range, concave/convex distinctions, and actual reflected paths versus backward extensions.
intent.source_solution: The pre-option frozen solution defines the principal focus in the paraxial model as the axial meeting point of reflected paths, or their backward extensions, for near-axis rays initially parallel to the principal axis. A concave mirror's reflected rays actually converge on the incident side, producing a real principal focus in front. A convex mirror's reflected rays diverge on that side, while their backward extensions meet behind, producing a virtual principal focus. Actual reflected rays do not pass through that virtual point. At a small height y the normal tilt is approximately y/R and the reflected deviation approximately 2y/R, giving a first-order focus distance of magnitude R/2 rather than the curvature-center distance R. No exact common point is asserted for arbitrary wide spherical-mirror beams.
intent.unit_reason: The source definition couples both mirror curvatures with real paths and virtual extensions. One native single question compares complete concave/convex classifications without separate binary items for each mirror or property. This is mathematically independent of the reflection-law source task, so the two sources support two response units.
limitations: Recognizing a definition does not demonstrate unaided complete oral or written recitation of the principal focus and concave/convex real/virtual distinctions.
Only the explicit paraxial model is used, without exact convergence claims for arbitrary wide beams or inferred source-image curvatures or values.
The internal R/2 derivation is independent mathematical checking, not a supplied source-image measurement or additional numerical learner task.
No solved construction or previous Q3 draft is consulted as a definition.

rationales.derivation: A concave mirror reflects paraxial axis-parallel rays toward an actual intersection in front. A convex mirror makes them diverge, with only their extensions meeting behind. This statement swaps the converging and diverging behavior of the two curvatures.
rationales.misconception: Exchange how concave and convex surfaces bend parallel rays, then consistently classify the swapped extension intersection as virtual and actual intersection as real.

rationales.derivation: A convex mirror's actual reflected rays diverge in front, rather than actually meeting behind. The behind-mirror intersection belongs to backward extensions and is virtual. The correct concave clause does not make the whole definition correct.
rationales.misconception: Treat the backward extensions of convex-mirror reflected rays as paths physically traversed by light, then apply an intersection-means-real-convergence rule to call the virtual focus real.

rationales.derivation: Concave-mirror local normals reflect near-axis parallel light toward an actual axial intersection on the incident side, yielding a real focus. Convex-mirror reflection diverges, with backward extensions converging on the axis behind the mirror, yielding a virtual focus. Both conclusions use the stem's paraxial approximation.

The curvature center lies on the spherical surface normals but is not the axis-parallel beam's principal focus. Small-angle reflection doubles the normal tilt, giving a paraxial focus distance of magnitude R/2 rather than the curvature-center distance R.
rationales.misconception: Transfer the fact that spherical surface normals meet at the curvature center to reflected axis-parallel rays, taking the normal intersection as the focus and omitting reflection's doubled deviation.

view.stem: In a paraxial concave-mirror imaging model, consider rays from the same off-axis object point. Every incident ray discussed is within the paraxial range and actually reaches a reflecting part of the mirror. Which incident-to-reflected ray correspondences are correct?

options.text: An incident ray through the focus is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
An incident ray through the center of curvature is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
An incident ray striking the pole has a reflected ray symmetric to the incident ray about the principal axis.
An incident ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected back along its original straight line.
An incident ray through the focus is reflected back along its original straight line.
An incident ray through the center of curvature is reflected back along its original straight line.
An incident ray striking the pole has a reflected ray directed along the line through the center of curvature.
An incident ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected through the focus.

intent.task: Collectively identify the four convenient incident rays and their reflected paths, rather than turn four definition entries into four yes/no questions.
intent.source_solution: The complete source solution was frozen before alternatives were constructed. A ray through the center of curvature follows the local normal and retraces its original straight path. A paraxial ray through the focus is reflected parallel to the principal axis. At the pole, the principal axis is the normal, making the incident and reflected rays symmetric about that axis. An axis-parallel paraxial incident ray is reflected through the focus. In the supplied model, two actually reflected, noncoincident convenient rays from the same object point that uniquely locate an intersection suffice to locate its image. A hole supplies no reflection, so the rays must reach reflecting surface. These statements are not extended to exact convergence of arbitrary wide beams or other unstated spherical-mirror cases.
intent.unit_reason: The written task requests a collective choice of convenient rays. One native multiple question preserves all four incident-condition/reflection distinctions together. Eight candidate correspondences express four correct laws and four reproducible mistaken derivations; they are not eight separate items, and printed rows do not dictate the item count. Actual surface availability and two-ray sufficiency are checked separately as one complete construction-policy judgment.
limitations: Recognizing correct correspondences does not demonstrate unaided recall and written production of the four rays and their explanations.
Independent ray-diagram production is not assessed; the selected written task asks which rays are convenient, not submission of a drawing.

The stem explicitly restricts the model to paraxial concave-mirror rays that reach reflecting surface. It neither asserts exact convergence of arbitrary wide beams nor supplies unseen source geometry.

rationales.derivation: An axis-parallel paraxial incident ray is reflected through the focus. Reversing that path makes a ray approaching the mirror through the focus reflect parallel to the principal axis, also matching the selected focus-ray definition.

The center-of-curvature ray follows the local normal and retraces its incoming line. For the stated off-axis object point, that line is not parallel to the principal axis, so the claimed parallel reflected path does not follow.
rationales.misconception: Replace the center of curvature by the focus in the incident condition, then incorrectly apply the focus-to-axis-parallel reflection rule to obtain this correspondence.

rationales.derivation: At the pole, the local normal is the principal axis. Equal incidence and reflection angles make the incident and reflected rays symmetric about that axis in the construction plane.

An axis-parallel ray from an off-axis object reaches the sphere away from the axis, where it is generally not along the local normal. Its paraxial reflected path passes through the focus rather than retracing the incoming line.
rationales.misconception: Treat the pole's principal-axis normal as a common normal everywhere on the curved surface. Since the incident ray is axis-parallel, incorrectly call it normal incidence at any surface point and apply the retracing rule.

rationales.derivation: Passing through the focus does not make the ray normal to the spherical surface at the point of incidence. Its paraxial reflected ray is axis-parallel; the line from the off-axis object through the focus is generally a different line.
rationales.misconception: Mistake the focus for the center of curvature, interpret the focus-directed incident ray as normal incidence, and incorrectly apply the center-of-curvature retracing rule.

rationales.derivation: The line from a spherical surface point to the center of curvature is its local normal. The center-of-curvature ray therefore has zero incidence and reflection angles and returns in the reverse direction along the same straight line.

The line from the pole through the center of curvature is the principal axis. A ray arriving at the pole from the stated off-axis point makes a nonzero angle with that normal and reflects at the same angle instead of automatically following the normal.
rationales.misconception: Correctly identify the pole's normal through the center of curvature, but then equate every reflected ray with that normal. Discard equality of incidence and reflection angles and obtain this center-directed reflected line.

rationales.derivation: Within the explicitly stated paraxial concave-mirror model, the focus is the location through which axis-parallel incident rays pass after reflection. This rule does not assert exact convergence of arbitrary wide beams.

view.stem: In a paraxial concave-mirror real-image construction, a central hole lets a ray from an off-axis object point pass through where it was directed toward the pole. Three other convenient rays, through the center of curvature, through the focus, and parallel to the principal axis, all reach reflecting surface, and their reflected paths are pairwise noncoincident. Which procedure can locate this object's image point using actually reflected rays?

options.text: Require the common intersection of all three remaining reflected lines; any two reflected lines are insufficient to locate the image point.
Use the reflection of the pole-directed ray passing through the hole and one remaining reflected line; apply the pole's reflection rule at the hole.
Use the intersection of any two of the three remaining reflected lines; do not treat the ray passing through the hole as a reflected ray.
Use just one of the remaining reflected lines as the position constraint; that line alone uniquely locates the image point.

intent.task: Judge a complete two-ray construction procedure subject to actual reflecting-surface availability, distinguishing sufficient two-line data, an unnecessary third-line requirement, one-line underdetermination, and a nonexistent hole reflection.
intent.source_solution: The source solution was frozen before alternatives: a center-of-curvature ray retraces its path, a focus ray reflects axis-parallel, a pole ray reflects symmetrically about the axis, and an axis-parallel ray reflects through the focus. These are used only in the seed's paraxial concave-mirror imaging range. Two actually reflected, noncoincident convenient rays from the same object point locate its real image by their intersection; a third ray is a check, not a necessity. A central hole supplies no reflected ray, so choose two rays reflected by the remaining surface. One reflected line gives a locus rather than a unique location.
intent.unit_reason: This checks two-ray sufficiency and real-surface availability from the selected definition context, distinct from the other item's four ray correspondences. One native single question compares complete construction policies instead of separate yes/no fragments about a third ray and reflection at a hole. No fixed item quota is imposed.
limitations: Recognizing the correct procedure does not demonstrate independently writing or drawing a complete two-ray construction.

The central hole, three available other convenient rays, and noncoincident reflected paths are explicitly stated candidate conditions grounded in the definition's availability principle, not geometry inferred from an unseen source image.
The judgment is limited to the declared paraxial real-image construction model. It does not infer a hole size, beam width, distance, or other unknown source parameter.

rationales.derivation: Two noncoincident reflected lines from the same object point already uniquely locate the image in the stated real-image model. A third can pass through the same point as a check, but this does not make two insufficient.
rationales.misconception: Turn checking the common image point with a third ray into a necessary condition for locating it. Require all three and incorrectly reject an already sufficient pair.

rationales.derivation: The ray through the hole does not reach reflecting surface, so it has no actual reflected path at the pole. The procedure uses a nonexistent reflection as a position constraint.
rationales.misconception: Apply the pole rule solely because the ray points toward the geometric pole, ignoring that the pole is a hole rather than reflecting surface. Draw that fictitious reflection and intersect it with another reflected line.

rationales.derivation: All three remaining convenient rays actually reflect, and their paths are noncoincident. In the paraxial real-image model they pass through the same image point, so any pair uniquely locates it by intersection without inventing a reflection at the hole.

One reflected line contains many possible positions and supplies no second independent position constraint. The ordinary ray construction requires a second noncoincident reflected line and their intersection.
rationales.misconception: Confuse a directional path constraint with a complete position constraint, claiming a unique image point along a line before obtaining an intersection with a second path.
